variants.title: Run the pipeline
variants.context: A tokenizer pipeline is ordered: normalize text under a declared Unicode policy, pre-tokenize to expose candidate boundaries, segment into vocabulary pieces with learned rules, and post-process by inserting trusted special tokens and producing masks and offsets.
variants.prompt: Text enters the tokenizer. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Segment into pieces from the fixed vocabulary using BPE merges, WordPiece rules, or unigram scores.
Normalize under a declared Unicode policy such as NFC or case folding.
Post-process: insert trusted special tokens and produce masks, type IDs, and offsets.
Pre-tokenize to expose candidate boundaries such as whitespace, punctuation, digits, or bytes.

variants.hint: Normalization can change code points and offsets before anything else happens.
variants.explanation: Normalize → pre-tokenize → segment → post-process. The final IDs index the embedding matrix.

variants.title: Run the pipeline
variants.context: A tokenizer pipeline is ordered: normalize text under a declared Unicode policy, pre-tokenize to expose candidate boundaries, segment into vocabulary pieces with learned rules, and post-process by inserting trusted special tokens and producing masks and offsets.
variants.prompt: A chat template is applied. Put the stages in order, noting where role markers enter.

items.text: Insert role and control IDs through the trusted template, never from user strings.
Segment the user text into ordinary vocabulary pieces.

variants.hint: Special tokens enter in post-processing through a trusted API.
variants.explanation: A literal string resembling a control marker must not gain authority.

variants.title: Run the pipeline
variants.context: A tokenizer pipeline is ordered: normalize text under a declared Unicode policy, pre-tokenize to expose candidate boundaries, segment into vocabulary pieces with learned rules, and post-process by inserting trusted special tokens and producing masks and offsets.
variants.prompt: Offsets are needed for redaction. Put the stages in order and note where offsets are produced.

items.text: Post-process, emitting offsets in a named unit relative to original or normalized text.
Normalize; this may change the mapping to the original text.

variants.hint: Record the offset unit and which text it refers to.
variants.explanation: Never compare offsets from two libraries until units and normalization stages are aligned.

variants.title: Keep the contract
variants.context: A tokenizer and a model checkpoint form one contract: normalization, vocabulary, IDs, special tokens, and templates must match training. A valid ID from another vocabulary selects the wrong embedding without an error. Untrusted text must never gain control-token authority.
variants.prompt: A team loads a checkpoint with a different tokenizer that happens to have the same vocabulary size. What happens?
options: The loader raises a vocabulary mismatch error and refuses to start the model.
Nothing changes, because equal vocabulary sizes mean both tokenizers index the same rows.
Valid IDs select the wrong embedding rows and quality degrades with no error raised.
optionFeedback: Nothing in the loader compares vocabularies, and every ID is a legal index into the table, so no error is raised.
Two vocabularies of equal size can still assign different spellings to the same integer.
Tokenizer and checkpoint are one contract, and a legal index is not a correct index.
variants.hint: What does token ID i select?
variants.explanation: Ship one immutable bundle with tokenizer, vocabulary, and special tokens.

variants.title: Keep the contract
variants.context: A tokenizer and a model checkpoint form one contract: normalization, vocabulary, IDs, special tokens, and templates must match training. A valid ID from another vocabulary selects the wrong embedding without an error. Untrusted text must never gain control-token authority.
variants.prompt: A user types the literal string <|system|> into a message. What must the pipeline do?
options: Reject the request, since control-looking text is always an injection attempt.
Encode it as ordinary content so the string never gains system authority.
Parse it into the real system control ID so the template matches training.
optionFeedback: Blocking every message that merely mentions a marker string throws away legitimate text and is not what keeps authority out.
Control IDs enter only through the trusted template, so the literal string stays content.
That is the injection path, because user text would gain system authority.
variants.explanation: Configure whether special-looking strings are allowed, rejected, or treated as text; library defaults differ.

variants.title: Keep the contract
variants.context: A tokenizer and a model checkpoint form one contract: normalization, vocabulary, IDs, special tokens, and templates must match training. A valid ID from another vocabulary selects the wrong embedding without an error. Untrusted text must never gain control-token authority.
variants.prompt: Decoding the IDs reproduces readable text. Does that prove the original string survived?
options: No, because normalization may have removed distinctions before segmentation ran.
Yes, because encoding and decoding are a lossless round trip by construction.
Yes, provided a reviewer reads the decoded text and sees no visible change.
optionFeedback: Decoding is useful for inspection, not proof that the exact input survived.
Nothing guarantees losslessness, and NFKC or case folding drops information on purpose.
Visual sameness hides removed code-point distinctions such as combining marks.
variants.explanation: Decoding is useful for inspection, not proof of preservation.

variants.title: Budget the context
variants.context: system + tools + history + retrieved evidence + user input + output reserve ≤ context window. The embedding table has V × d entries. Do not use a universal four-characters-per-token rule; count with the production tokenizer per slice.
variants.prompt: The window is 8,000 tokens. System instructions use 500, tool schemas 300, history 1,200, user input 400, and the output reserve is 1,000. How many tokens remain for retrieved evidence?
variants.hint: Subtract each component from the window.

mistakes.feedback: The output reserve also comes out of the window.

variants.title: Budget the context
variants.context: system + tools + history + retrieved evidence + user input + output reserve ≤ context window. The embedding table has V × d entries. Do not use a universal four-characters-per-token rule; count with the production tokenizer per slice.
variants.prompt: A vocabulary has 50,000 entries and embeddings are 4,096 wide. How many numbers are in the embedding table?
variants.explanation: 50,000 × 4,096 = 204,800,000 values; every vocabulary entry costs an embedding row.

variants.title: Budget the context
variants.context: system + tools + history + retrieved evidence + user input + output reserve ≤ context window. The embedding table has V × d entries. Do not use a universal four-characters-per-token rule; count with the production tokenizer per slice.
variants.prompt: A 12,000-character input would be about 3,000 tokens at four characters per token, but this script expands three times more than English. How many tokens should you expect?
variants.hint: Apply the expansion factor to the naive estimate.
variants.explanation: 3,000 × 3 = 9,000 tokens; count with the production tokenizer instead of a universal rule.

mistakes.feedback: Multiply the token estimate, not the character count, by three.

variants.title: Measure by slice
variants.context: Measure multilingual text and code separately: low-resource scripts can expand into many tokens; whitespace is not a universal boundary; NFKC or case folding can erase distinctions; code and structured text need dedicated tests.
variants.prompt: An admission control uses four characters per token for every language. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing goes wrong, because four characters per token holds across scripts.
English prose is undercounted, so English requests are rejected too early.
Low-resource scripts and code expand far more, so limits are breached silently.
optionFeedback: There is no universal ratio, since the number depends on the tokenizer, script, and content type.
English prose is roughly where the rule came from, so it is the slice the rule fits best.
An average dominated by English prose hides severe expansion in other slices.
variants.hint: Which traffic does the average hide?
variants.explanation: Report distributions by language and content type.

variants.title: Measure by slice
variants.context: Measure multilingual text and code separately: low-resource scripts can expand into many tokens; whitespace is not a universal boundary; NFKC or case folding can erase distinctions; code and structured text need dedicated tests.
variants.prompt: NFKC normalization is applied globally to save vocabulary. What can it break?
options: Nothing, since NFKC only merges visually identical forms of the same text.
Only emoji sequences, which lose their variation selectors after folding.
Identifiers, passwords, legal text, and code where exact code points matter.
optionFeedback: NFKC deliberately erases compatibility distinctions, so it is not a no-op on real content.
Emoji are one narrow case, and identifiers, passwords, and code lose far more.
Normalization erases distinctions that some content classes need.
variants.hint: Which content depends on exact code points?
variants.explanation: Choose normalization per content class with evidence.

variants.title: Measure by slice
variants.context: Measure multilingual text and code separately: low-resource scripts can expand into many tokens; whitespace is not a universal boundary; NFKC or case folding can erase distinctions; code and structured text need dedicated tests.
variants.prompt: Source code is tokenized by a prose-trained tokenizer. What should you test?
options: Only the comments, since the rest of the file is ordinary punctuation.
Indentation, newlines, casing, underscores, operators, and long identifiers.
Nothing extra, because code is text and the prose measurements already cover it.
optionFeedback: Comments are the prose-like part, and the structural characters are where splitting goes wrong.
Structure in code carries meaning the prose tokenizer may split inefficiently.
Code is a distinct slice and needs its own token-count measurements.
variants.hint: Which characters carry structure in code?
variants.explanation: Dates, decimals, UUIDs, and JSON escapes also need dedicated tests.

variants.title: Choose the selection policy
variants.context: Truncation drops tokens; chunking creates multiple bounded sequences. Protect trusted instructions, the current task, and the output reserve before optional history; return metadata about what was removed; overlap in chunking is duplicated cost.
variants.prompt: The request exceeds the window. What should be protected first?
options: Everything equally, trimming each section by the same percentage.
Trusted instructions, the current task, and the output reserve.
The oldest history, so the conversation keeps its original framing.
optionFeedback: Proportional trimming still cuts the instructions and the output reserve, which the request cannot lose.
Truncation is an information-selection policy, so protect what the answer depends on.
Old history is the most optional part of the budget, not the most protected.
variants.hint: Which tokens can you not afford to lose?
variants.explanation: Return metadata stating what was removed.

variants.title: Choose the selection policy
variants.context: Truncation drops tokens; chunking creates multiple bounded sequences. Protect trusted instructions, the current task, and the output reserve before optional history; return metadata about what was removed; overlap in chunking is duplicated cost.
variants.prompt: Right truncation dropped the conclusion of a document. What went wrong?
options: The truncation side was chosen without asking where the key content sits.
Nothing went wrong, because right truncation is the standard default.
The tokenizer miscounted the document and cut more than the limit required.
optionFeedback: Decide left, right, or semantic priority deliberately for each content shape.
A default is still a policy choice, and this one discarded the conclusion.
Truncation is a policy applied after counting, not a tokenizer bug.
variants.hint: Where does the critical content sit?
variants.explanation: Silent truncation makes missing evidence look like model failure.

variants.title: Choose the selection policy
variants.context: Truncation drops tokens; chunking creates multiple bounded sequences. Protect trusted instructions, the current task, and the output reserve before optional history; return metadata about what was removed; overlap in chunking is duplicated cost.
variants.prompt: Chunks overlap by 30% to preserve cross-boundary evidence. What is the cost?
options: Answer quality drops, because repeated text confuses the retrieval ranking.
Overlap is duplicated input, so it duplicates latency and token cost.
There is no cost, since the overlapping tokens are deduplicated before billing.
optionFeedback: Overlap usually helps recall across boundaries, and the price is paid in tokens rather than quality.
Use overlap only when cross-boundary evidence needs it.
Nothing deduplicates them, so every overlapping token is sent and paid for.
variants.hint: What does each overlapping token cost?
variants.explanation: Split on structure first, then enforce limits with the production tokenizer.
